Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- More than one million people in Darfur are at risk of losing food, water and shelter in coming months, following the expulsion of international aid groups by Sudan's government, the United Nations' chief humanitarian coordinator said Tuesday. A Doctors without Borders medic helps a sick child in a Darfur refugee camp. The statement by coordinator John Holmes comes after a joint U.N.-Sudanese assessment of the situation. The information was gathered from March 11-18 in hopes of stemming further troubles in Darfur after Sudan's government expelled 13 international relief organizations from the wartorn region. The announcement came on the same day that President Omar al-Bashir, now an indicted war criminal, ignored the threat of arrest by traveling abroad to Eritrea. Also Tuesday, a Sudanese staffer working for a Canadian relief group was shot dead in Darfur. A full report of the assessment will be released soon, according to the U.N., but an executive summary and recommendations were made available on Tuesday. "While a significant effort is being made by the government, by the U.N., by the NGOs [nongovernmental organizations] which are left, to plug some of the immediate gaps in these areas, these are at the same time, 'Band-Aid' solutions, not long term solutions," Holmes said. The U.N. estimates that 1.5 million people in Darfur are dependent on healthcare support, 1.1 million need regular food aid, and another 1 million are in need of clean drinking water. The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which is still allowed to operate in Sudan, is carrying out a one-time-only distribution program in March and April, but that new partners will be needed to continue delivering food after April. After the International Criminal Court charged Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity on March 4, Khartoum expelled 13 international aid agencies and revoked the permits of three organizations in the country. Bashir -- the first sitting head of state to be charged with war crimes by the court -- has continued to say that humanitarian efforts in the country should be "Sudanized." "Within a year, we don't want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen," he said at a rally a week after his arrest warrant was issued. Holmes said that 13,000 to 14,000 aid workers in the region already were Sudanese nationals. Holmes said the cooperation and technical help from the Sudanese government on the assessment was a good step forward. But he called it "only the first of many steps if the people in Darfur are not going to suffer major consequences from these expulsions." Sudan's U.N. Ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly said he has information implicating the ousted organizations in activities contrary to their humanitarian missions. He has yet to make any of that information public. One claim is that some organizations acted as spies for the International Criminal Court. Holmes denied those allegations, saying they remain unfounded. "Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence," he said. "In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be done." The British aid organization, Oxfam, one of the agencies expelled from Sudan, released a statement in response to Tuesday's findings. "Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time," the statement said. "As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters, in flood-prone locations where latrines can fill and overflow, will become at extreme risk of disease and death. "With the humanitarian capacity reduced by nearly 50 percent, responding to such emergency scenarios will be an enormous challenge for others to tackle," Oxfam said.

outputs.L1:
UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- More than one million people in Darfur risk losing access to food, water, and shelter in the coming months following the expulsion of international aid organizations by Sudan's government, the United Nations' chief humanitarian coordinator announced Tuesday.

The statement from coordinator John Holmes follows a joint U.N.-Sudanese assessment of the situation, conducted from March 11 to 18 in an effort to mitigate further crisis in Darfur after Khartoum expelled 13 international relief organizations from the war-torn region. The announcement coincided with President Omar al-Bashir—now an indicted war criminal—defying the threat of arrest by traveling abroad to Eritrea. Also on Tuesday, a Sudanese staff member working for a Canadian relief organization was shot dead in Darfur.

While a comprehensive report on the assessment is expected soon, the U.N. released an executive summary and accompanying recommendations on Tuesday. "While a significant effort is being made by the government, by the U.N., and by the NGOs [nongovernmental organizations] that remain, to address some of the immediate gaps in these areas, these are, at best, 'Band-Aid' solutions—not long-term fixes," Holmes said.

According to U.N. estimates, 1.5 million people in Darfur depend on healthcare support, 1.1 million require regular food assistance, and another 1 million lack access to clean drinking water. Tuesday's summary noted that the World Food Programme, which continues to operate in Sudan, is conducting a one-time distribution effort in March and April—but that new partners will be essential to sustain food delivery beyond that point.

The expulsions followed the International Criminal Court's March 4 indictment of Bashir on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity, after which Khartoum expelled 13 international aid agencies and revoked the operating permits of three others. Bashir—the first sitting head of state to be charged with war crimes by the ICC—has consistently maintained that humanitarian efforts within the country should be "Sudanized." "Within a year, we don't want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen," he declared at a rally held a week after his arrest warrant was issued.

Holmes noted that between 13,000 and 14,000 aid workers currently operating in the region are already Sudanese nationals.

He characterized the Sudanese government's cooperation and technical assistance during the assessment as a positive step forward, though he cautioned that it represents "only the first of many steps if the people of Darfur are to avoid suffering severe consequences from these expulsions."

Sudan's U.N. Ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly claimed to possess evidence implicating the expelled organizations in activities inconsistent with their humanitarian mandates—including allegations that some groups served as informants for the International Criminal Court. However, he has yet to make any such evidence public.

Holmes rejected these allegations as unsubstantiated. "Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence," he said. "In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be conducted."

Oxfam, the British aid organization among those expelled from Sudan, issued a statement responding to Tuesday's findings: "Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time. As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters—in flood-prone locations where latrines can overflow—will face extreme risk of disease and death."

The statement continued: "With humanitarian capacity reduced by nearly 50 percent, responding to such emergency scenarios will pose an enormous challenge for those who remain."

# Humanitarian Crisis Deepens in Darfur Following Aid Group Expulsions

More than one million people across Darfur now face the imminent loss of critical access to food, clean water, and shelter, as the fallout from Sudan's government decision to expel international aid organizations continues to unfold. The move has left a substantial gap in humanitarian services in a region already struggling with years of conflict and displacement.

In response to the growing emergency, the United Nations and Sudanese government officials conducted a joint crisis assessment from March 11 to March 18. The evaluation was specifically designed to identify and address the service gaps created after 13 relief organizations were forced out of Darfur, effectively dismantling much of the humanitarian infrastructure that vulnerable populations had come to depend on.

John Holmes, the U.N.'s humanitarian coordinator, offered a sobering assessment of the current state of relief efforts. He characterized existing measures as little more than temporary "Band-Aid" solutions—stopgap interventions that fall far short of the sustainable, long-term support systems that the population urgently requires. His comments underscore growing concern among international officials that without a comprehensive strategy, the situation could deteriorate further.

Adding a striking political dimension to the unfolding crisis, Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir made a defiant gesture on the very day the assessment was announced. Despite having been indicted by the International Criminal Court on war crimes charges—and facing the ongoing threat of arrest—al-Bashir traveled to Eritrea, seemingly undeterred by international legal pressure and signaling his continued disregard for the court's authority.

The scale of humanitarian need in Darfur remains staggering. According to U.N. estimates, approximately 1.5 million people currently require healthcare support, while 1.1 million depend on regular food assistance to survive. Compounding these challenges, an estimated 1 million residents lack access to clean drinking water, raising serious concerns about disease outbreaks and further deterioration of public health conditions across the region.

As the assessment findings are analyzed, humanitarian officials face mounting pressure to develop solutions that go beyond emergency stopgaps and instead establish durable systems capable of meeting the needs of Darfur's population over the long term—all while navigating the complex political realities posed by a government resistant to international accountability.

# Sudan Faces Humanitarian Crisis After Aid Group Expulsions

In March 2009, the government of Sudan expelled 13 major international aid organizations from the country, a retaliatory move that followed the International Criminal Court's decision to indict President Omar al-Bashir on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Darfur region. The expulsion of these organizations—which had been responsible for delivering critical humanitarian services including food distribution, medical care, water sanitation, and shelter assistance—immediately raised alarm among international observers and humanitarian officials who warned of a looming crisis for the millions of displaced people still suffering from the effects of the prolonged Darfur conflict.

In response to mounting concerns, the United Nations partnered with Sudanese government officials to conduct a comprehensive joint assessment of the humanitarian situation on the ground. This collaborative evaluation was designed to systematically examine how the sudden departure of these aid groups had affected ongoing relief operations throughout Darfur, and to pinpoint specific areas where critical gaps in service delivery had emerged or were likely to emerge in the near future.

The findings of this assessment painted a troubling picture of the region's humanitarian outlook. According to the report, more than one million people across Darfur now face the imminent risk of losing access to basic necessities—including food supplies, clean drinking water, and adequate shelter—within the coming months if adequate solutions are not urgently implemented. The assessment further revealed that the stopgap measures currently being used to bridge the service gap left by the expelled organizations were fundamentally inadequate for long-term sustainability. Officials characterized these interim efforts as mere "Band-Aid" solutions, emphasizing that while they might provide temporary relief, they were incapable of addressing the deeper, systemic challenges posed by the loss of experienced and well-established aid infrastructure.

This sobering assessment has intensified calls within the international community for swift action to recruit new humanitarian partners capable of stepping into the void left behind by the expelled organizations. Without such intervention, aid workers and U.N. officials warn that the humanitarian crisis in Darfur could deepen significantly, placing already vulnerable populations at even greater risk as the window for implementing sustainable solutions continues to narrow.

# The United Nations and CNN: Global Governance Meets Global Media

The United Nations, founded in 1945 in the aftermath of World War II, stands as the world's largest intergovernmental organization dedicated to maintaining international peace and security, fostering friendly relations among nations, and promoting social progress and human rights. With 193 member states, the UN operates through various bodies including the General Assembly, Security Council, and numerous specialized agencies that address issues ranging from humanitarian crises to climate change.

CNN, launched in 1980 as the world's first 24-hour news channel, revolutionized global media by providing continuous news coverage across international borders. Its reach into millions of households worldwide has made it a significant player in shaping public perception of international events.

The relationship between these two institutions illustrates the important connection between global governance and global media. CNN has historically played a crucial role in covering UN proceedings, from Security Council debates to General Assembly sessions, bringing these often complex diplomatic discussions to a worldwide audience. Major UN initiatives, peacekeeping missions, humanitarian interventions, and international summits regularly receive coverage from CNN correspondents stationed at UN headquarters in New York and other key locations.

This media coverage serves several important functions. First, it provides transparency, allowing citizens around the world to witness international diplomacy in action rather than relying solely on official statements. Second, it can amplify humanitarian concerns, as CNN's coverage of crises addressed by UN agencies—such as refugee situations, famines, or conflicts—often influences public opinion and, subsequently, political will for international action.

However, the relationship isn't without tension. Critics have noted that media coverage, including CNN's, can sometimes oversimplify complex UN processes or focus disproportionately on dramatic conflicts rather than the UN's ongoing developmental and diplomatic work. The so-called "CNN effect"—a theory suggesting that real-time media coverage can pressure policymakers into action—has been debated extensively in relation to UN interventions, particularly during the 1990s in cases like Somalia and Rwanda.

In the digital age, both institutions continue to evolve. The UN has expanded its own digital communications strategies, while CNN has adapted to a fragmented media landscape with numerous competitors and social media platforms. Together, they represent the ongoing interplay between international institutions working toward global cooperation and the media organizations tasked with informing the public about these efforts.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about the humanitarian crisis in Darfur following Sudan's expulsion of international aid groups.
counterfactuals.output:
# Darfur Crisis Deepens as Sudan Expels Aid Groups, Leaving Millions Without Lifeline

**By CNN Staff**

EL FASHER, Sudan — The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Darfur has reached a new and dangerous inflection point after Sudanese authorities ordered the expulsion of several international aid organizations, cutting off critical assistance to millions of civilians trapped in a region already devastated by war, displacement, and famine.

Aid workers and humanitarian officials describe a rapidly deteriorating situation in which hospitals are shutting down, food distribution has ground to a halt, and displaced families are being left to fend for themselves amid ongoing violence between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

"We are watching a man-made famine unfold in real time, and now the very organizations trying to prevent mass starvation are being forced out," said one senior humanitarian official who requested anonymity to speak freely about the expulsions. "This is not just a setback — it could be the difference between life and death for hundreds of thousands of people."

## A Region Already on the Brink

Darfur has been at the epicenter of Sudan's civil war since fighting erupted in April 2023, with the RSF accused of carrying out ethnically targeted atrocities reminiscent of the genocide that gripped the region two decades ago. The United Nations has repeatedly warned that famine conditions already exist in parts of Darfur, particularly in and around the besieged city of El Fasher and the Zamzam displacement camp, once home to hundreds of thousands of people fleeing violence.

The expulsion of aid groups — which Sudanese authorities have justified on security grounds, accusing some organizations of bias or unauthorized activity — strips away what little infrastructure remained to deliver food, medical care, and clean water to a population pushed to the edge of survival.

"These camps were barely surviving before," said a nurse who worked with a now-expelled medical charity and fled to neighboring Chad. "Without international staff, without supplies coming in, I don't know what happens to the people we left behind."

## Millions Cut Off

According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, more than 24 million people across Sudan require humanitarian assistance, with Darfur among the hardest-hit regions. Aid groups estimate that the expulsions could affect access to food and medical care for several million people in North, South, and West Darfur alone.

Local volunteer networks and emergency response rooms — grassroots groups of Sudanese citizens who have stepped in to fill gaps left by the collapse of formal aid infrastructure — say they are being asked to do the impossible.

"We have no salaries, we have almost no supplies, and now the organizations that were supporting us are gone," said a volunteer coordinator in El Fasher, speaking via a spotty satellite connection. "People are coming to us dying of hunger and we have nothing to give them."

## International Reaction

The expulsions have drawn sharp condemnation from the United Nations and Western governments. UN Secretary-General António Guterres called on Sudanese authorities to "immediately reverse this decision," warning that the move violates international humanitarian law and could accelerate an already catastrophic loss of life.

The United States, the European Union, and several African nations have urged both warring parties — the Sudanese military government and the RSF — to guarantee unimpeded humanitarian access. But with the conflict showing no signs of resolution and mutual distrust running deep, diplomats say securing renewed access will be an uphill battle.

"There is a real risk that Darfur becomes a black hole — a place where atrocities and starvation happen completely out of view of the international community," said a Western diplomat involved in Sudan policy discussions.

## Fears of a Repeat of History

For many observers, the crisis carries painful echoes of the early 2000s, when Darfur became synonymous with genocide as government-backed militias, the Janjaweed — predecessors to today's RSF — carried out mass killings of non-Arab ethnic groups. Survivors and human rights monitors say many of the same patterns are reemerging, this time with even less international oversight.

Satellite imagery analyzed by researchers has shown evidence of mass graves and burned villages in areas controlled by the RSF, though independent verification remains difficult given restricted access to the region.

"The world said 'never again' after the last Darfur genocide," said a human rights researcher who has tracked the conflict since it began. "But without aid workers, without journalists, without any international presence, we may never even know the full scale of what is happening now."

## What Comes Next

Humanitarian organizations are scrambling to find alternative routes to deliver aid, including cross-border operations from Chad, though these efforts remain limited in scale and face their own logistical and security challenges.

For the millions of Darfuris trapped between famine and violence, the coming weeks may prove decisive. Aid officials warn that without a reversal of the expulsion order — or the establishment of alternative aid corridors — the death toll from starvation and disease could soon rival that of the conflict's direct violence.

"The world cannot say it didn't know," the humanitarian official said. "The warnings have been made. The question now is whether anyone will act before it's too late."

---

*This is a developing story. CNN will continue to update as more information becomes available.*

# UN Findings on Sudan's Expulsion of Aid Organizations from Darfur

## Background
In March 2009, Sudan expelled 13 international aid organizations from Darfur, shortly after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President Omar al-Bashir on charges related to war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Darfur conflict.

## Key UN Findings

**John Holmes**, the UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator, warned that the expulsions created severe gaps in humanitarian services for the estimated 4.7 million people affected by the Darfur conflict, including approximately 2.7 million internally displaced persons.

Holmes highlighted that the expelled organizations had been responsible for critical services including:
- Food distribution
- Clean water access
- Healthcare provision
- Sanitation services

He characterized the situation as creating dangerous gaps in the humanitarian safety net, warning that the withdrawal of these organizations—which had provided roughly half of the humanitarian assistance in the region—could not be easily replaced by remaining agencies or the Sudanese government's own capacity.

Holmes emphasized the urgency of the crisis, noting concerns that disruptions to water and health services in particular could lead to increased disease outbreaks and mortality rates among vulnerable populations, especially children.

# Aid Crisis Deepens in Darfur Following ICC Warrant

**KHARTOUM** — Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir's response to his International Criminal Court indictment has triggered a humanitarian crisis affecting more than a million people across Darfur, aid organizations warn, as the government's expulsion of relief agencies leaves critical gaps in food, medical care, and water services throughout the conflict-torn region.

## Background on the Indictment

The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Bashir in March 2009, marking the first time the court had sought the arrest of a sitting head of state. Prosecutors charged him with war crimes and crimes against humanity related to the conflict in Darfur, which began in 2003 when rebel groups took up arms against the government, accusing it of marginalizing the region's non-Arab population. The government's subsequent counterinsurgency campaign, carried out with allied militias, led to widespread allegations of atrocities against civilians.

## Government Response

Within hours of the warrant's announcement, Sudanese authorities ordered the expulsion of at least 13 international humanitarian organizations operating in Darfur, accusing them of collaborating with the ICC and compromising national security. Several Sudanese human rights and relief organizations were also shut down. The expelled groups reportedly included major providers of food aid, medical services, water and sanitation support, and shelter materials for displaced populations.

## Humanitarian Impact

Aid organizations and UN officials estimate that the expulsions have disrupted services for over a million people who depend on humanitarian assistance in Darfur's camps for internally displaced persons. Key concerns include:

- **Food security**: Disruption to food distribution networks serving displaced populations already dependent on international assistance
- **Medical care**: Loss of health clinics and medical staff providing basic and emergency care
- **Water and sanitation**: Reduced capacity to maintain clean water access, raising fears of disease outbreaks in crowded camps
- **Protection services**: Diminished monitoring and support for vulnerable groups, including women and children

Humanitarian coordinators have warned that the remaining aid infrastructure cannot absorb the caseload left by the departing organizations, raising fears of a rapid deterioration in conditions as the region moves toward hotter months when water and health needs typically intensify.

## International Reaction

The expulsions drew condemnation from the United Nations, Western governments, and international rights groups, who called on Khartoum to reverse the decision and allow humanitarian access to resume. Some diplomats have sought to negotiate compromises, including proposals for replacement organizations or expanded roles for remaining agencies, though aid groups caution that no substitute can quickly fill the gap left by experienced organizations with established networks in the region.

## Outlook

With the rainy season approaching and displacement camps already strained, aid officials describe the situation as increasingly urgent. Humanitarian agencies continue to press the Sudanese government for renewed access, while monitoring groups warn that prolonged restrictions could result in significant increases in preventable deaths from disease, malnutrition, and lack of medical care.

*This report reflects publicly available information on the situation as it developed in 2009. Readers seeking the most current details on Darfur's humanitarian situation should consult recent UN OCHA reports and established news outlets for updates.*

# UN, Sudanese Officials Complete Joint Assessment of Darfur Humanitarian Needs Following Aid Group Expulsions

**By CNN Wire Staff**

A joint assessment team comprising United Nations officials and Sudanese government representatives has completed a review of humanitarian needs in Darfur following the expulsion of several international aid organizations earlier this year, according to officials familiar with the mission.

The assessment comes amid mounting concern from humanitarian organizations that critical gaps in aid delivery have emerged since Sudan's government ordered more than a dozen aid groups to cease operations in the region. The expelled organizations had provided food, medical care, clean water, and other essential services to millions of displaced civilians across Darfur, where conflict has raged for years between government-aligned forces and rebel groups.

The joint review was intended to evaluate the current state of humanitarian operations and determine whether remaining aid organizations and government mechanisms can adequately meet the needs of vulnerable populations, including the estimated 2.7 million people displaced by the conflict.

Details of the assessment's specific findings have not been fully released, but the review is expected to inform decisions by the international community on how to proceed with aid delivery in the region.

**Oxfam Voices Concern**

Aid organizations that remain active in Sudan have expressed skepticism about whether the joint assessment can accurately capture the scale of unmet needs on the ground.

Oxfam, one of the humanitarian organizations continuing operations in the region, said the expulsions have already had a severe impact on the ability to deliver aid effectively. A spokesperson for the organization emphasized that gaps left by the departure of expelled groups have not been adequately filled by remaining agencies or government bodies.

The organization called for greater transparency regarding the assessment's methodology and urged that findings be made public promptly, warning that delays in addressing service gaps could have life-threatening consequences for displaced families heading into the coming months.

Humanitarian officials have long warned that Darfur's displaced population faces acute vulnerabilities, including malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and lack of access to clean water, particularly in remote camps where aid access has historically been difficult even before the expulsions.

**Background**
